author: SULAYMAN BOWLES
thesis: Separate search discovery, model development, and user-triggered fetching before selecting agent groups. Deployed rules express policy; logs and dated provider ranges support attribution, not proof of downstream use.

conclusion.title: Keep the policy claim narrower than the evidence
conclusion.content: Test the deployed groups and classify observed traffic with provider-specific guidance and dated ranges. A named-agent rule does not cover every client, prove compliance, or establish indexing, training exclusion, or citation.

evidenceBoundary: This guide documents published crawler controls as verified on July 14, 2026. A robots.txt rule expresses policy; it does not secure private content, authenticate a bot, or prove indexing, ranking, training exclusion, or answer-system citation.
content: AI search, model development, and user-opened URLs need separate decisions. Blocking a training token does not by itself block a provider’s search crawler or user-requested fetcher. The dated comparison below preserves the provider guidance reviewed for this guide; it is not a newly verified inventory.

Publish each named product token in its own intended /robots.txt group with Allow: / or Disallow: /, and retain the correct Sitemap line. [The protocol](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.html#section-2.2.1) requires case-insensitive product-token group matching; it separately says path matching should be case sensitive. Use the documented branded spellings without treating token casing as an access boundary.

Choose the outcome, select the groups, merge the existing file, and fetch production before inspecting logs. Robots rules guide cooperating clients; protect private files with authentication or server-side authorization regardless of those rules.

sections.title: Separate search, training, and user requests
paragraphs: Choose the intended outcome before copying a rule. Search discovery and model-development opt-out target different agents; user-requested fetching follows provider-specific behavior. Private files require an enforceable access boundary for every client, not another robots group.

sections.title: Compare purposes before tokens
paragraphs: Use the named product token rather than a versioned HTTP header. The table distinguishes search, model-development, and user-request roles at its stated verification date. In particular, user-triggered access may follow different robots behavior; do not infer compliance merely from the provider name.

sections.title: Merge the example with the host’s policy
paragraphs: Choose a template, then reconcile it with existing search-engine, media, path, and sitemap rules. Replace the example sitemap hostname. The broad block names only this guide’s agents; its user-fetch exceptions remain important, and private-path rules do not secure the underlying content.

codeExamples.title: Block listed AI agents
codeExamples.description: Blocks every AI-related agent named in this guide. No static list can cover every crawler, ChatGPT-User rules may not apply, and Perplexity-User generally ignores robots.txt, so enforce sensitive-content controls at authentication or the server edge.

sections.title: Check production and retain attribution uncertainty
paragraphs: Fetch every production /robots.txt endpoint and compare its returned groups with the committed file. Inspect current and rotated NGINX logs using the filter below. A token match records a claim; check its address against the provider’s dated JSON ranges before attributing traffic, and retain uncertainty when the evidence is insufficient.
bullets: Expected response: HTTP 200, text/plain, intended group, correct sitemap hostname.
Useful fields: timestamp, host, path, status, source address, complete User-Agent.
Interpretation rule: absence from the log does not prove a block succeeded.
